But that may be too late to neuter the anti-tax campaign. The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association is already gathering signatures and raising funds (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1059890&view=received).
“This was an attempt to cut us off early in the process, but since we’re moving forward I think the attempt to leverage this is not going to prevail,” Jon Coupal, the association’s president. “Their opportunity to ambush us is now over.”
That’s given local government groups billions of reasons to worry. Along with making it more challenging to raise revenue in the future, cities with existing high transfer taxes would see them slashed. Parcel taxes currently on the books that were approved by majorities of less than two-thirds would be similarly nixed.
Cities would lose between $2 billion and $3 billion each year if the measure becomes law, according to an analysis commissioned by the League of California Cities, a lobbying group. That includes hundreds of millions of dollars in foregone funding dedicated for new housing and homelessness services in Los Angeles and Santa Monica. But it also includes hundreds of millions more for cities that don’t use these transfer dollars for new, specific purposes and projects, but simply to top up their budgets.
The City of Berkeley, for example, stands to lose between $33 million and $63 million, according to the League’s analysis. That’s the equivalent of between 15-30% of the town’s general fund.
California’s favorite fight
Californians have been having some version of this fight for nearly half a century.
In 1978, voters passed Proposition 13, which capped property taxes and put strict limits on local and state governments’ ability to raise revenue. Defending, rolling back and revising (https://calmatters.org/politics/2020/10/prop-13-family-tree/) those limits in court battles and subsequent state ballot measure campaigns is now a storied California political tradition.
The latest chapter began in 2017 when the California Supreme Court (https://calmatters.org/economy/2017/08/california-taxes-two-step/) ruled in a case against the southern California city of Upland that citizen-initiated special tax measures only need to get more than 50% of the vote to pass. Up until that point it was presumed that the required threshold was the much more electorally formidable two-thirds.
Since then cities and counties have passed two dozen of these measures by margins of less than two-thirds. That includes taxes on parcels, sales and gross receipts that have been used to fund local schools, parks, street repairs and housing and that have been put on the ballot by homeless advocates, environmentalists and organized labor groups. It also includes Measure ULA.
And since then, business groups have been clambering to close the “Upland loophole.”
“This is now the vehicle for unions and others to be able to try and pass new taxes on targeted business sectors using a majority vote,” said Lapsely. “That only hurts job growth.”
Over that same period some cities have also turned to transfer taxes as a new source of revenue. It’s a fiscal avenue only available to a select number of cities. Under state law, most municipalities max out their transfer taxes at 55 cents for every $1,000 in sale value. But for “charter cities” — local governments with their own municipal constitution — there is no upper limit. Twenty-six have taken advantage of that fiscal opportunity.
They include Santa Monica, which passed its own version of a high-value transfer tax (Measure GS) in 2022, and Los Angeles. Voters in cities across the San Francisco Bay Area have voted to make more modest or incremental hikes over the last 10 years.
Electoral hurdles to come
The transfer tax trend has particularly irked landlords and real estate developers.
Last year, they joined forces with anti-tax advocates and other business groups to rein in both types of bothersome taxation with a ballot measure. The California Supreme Court took the unusual step of striking it (https://calmatters.org/politics/2024/06/california-taxes-supreme-court-ballot/) from the 2024 ballot, ruling that it proposed too “substantial” a change to state government to be enacted by a mere ballot measure.
This year’s version is much more carefully targeted making it less likely to hit this same constitutional snag.
But even if the signature gathering effort is successful, the Howard Jarvis campaign has its work cut out for it — even for a conservative-coded measure in reliably blue California. In late 2023, the Legislature floated its own head-spinning ballot measure (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202320240aca13) that would require future initiatives that want to hike the threshold needed to pass other measures (see: the business-backed measure) to meet that same higher threshold (in this case, two-thirds) before becoming law.
That effort to hoist the Howard Jarvis Taxpayer Association on its own petard is already slated for the November 2026 election. If it passes, it would apply to any other measures also on the ballot.

California is about to have a massive fight over taxes. Here’s why Los Angeles is the frontline
by
Ben Christopher (https://calmatters.org/author/ben-christopher/)
October 6, 2025 Updated October 7, 2025

In summary
A low-tax advocacy group seems intent on making the Los Angeles “mansion tax” the face of their statewide tax-capping ballot measure campaign.
Welcome to CalMatters, the only nonprofit newsroom devoted solely to covering issues that affect all Californians. Sign up for WhatMatters (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/whatmatters) to receive the latest news and commentary on the most important issues in the Golden State.
In 2022, the Los Angeles electorate voted to slap the sale of mansions and other high-value real estate deals across the city with a hefty tax.
Locals have been debating Measure ULA ever since. Supporters call it a vital lifeline for the city’s unhoused and housing insecure who stand to benefit from the hundreds of millions of dollars the initiative has already raked in. Critics call it an economic own-goal that has choked off new apartment construction in a city where new housing is in excruciatingly short supply.
That debate is about to go statewide.
The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, a low tax advocacy group, is currently gathering signatures to put a measure on California’s November 2026 ballot. A central part of their pitch: No more Measure ULAs.
The proposed constitutional amendment takes aim at two types of taxation common across California:
Transfer taxes on the sale of real estate. The measure would cap rates at a little more than one-twentieth of one percent of the value of the property. Los Angeles’ highest rate is one hundred-times higher.
Local tax measures put on the ballot by voter-backed campaigns (as opposed to those put there by city councils) that are earmarked for a particular purpose. The tax-capping proposal would raise the electoral support needed to pass these types of “special” tax measures to two-thirds, up from a simple majority of more than 50%.
Municipal governments across the state stand to lose billions of dollars (with taxpayers standing to save just as much) if the measure ultimately succeeds. Voter-proposed tax hikes have been approved by simple majorities in cities and counties across California. Transfer tax hikes have also been a popular funding source for certain local governments.
Measure ULA, which 58% of Los Angeles voters backed in 2022, happens to be both. The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association and its political allies appear happy to make it the face of the statewide campaign.
Putting a lid on both citizen-initiated tax measures and high transfer taxes “is something that we have always had as a priority,” said Rob Lapsely, president of the California Business Roundtable, a coalition that has yet to take a formal position on the measure but which backed an earlier version. “The question was, ‘can we actually find the right opportunity?’”
“And then suddenly, along came Measure ULA.”
The fight over the “mansion tax”
The City of Los Angeles’ measure was sold to voters as a “mansion tax,” because it sticks new, elevated transfer fee rates on only the highest value sales: 4% on properties between $5 million and $10 million and 5.5% for those above that. Those numbers have inched up with inflation. All sales below those thresholds are taxed at roughly half of one percent.

Since going into effect in 2023, the measure has raised some $830 million (https://housing.lacity.gov/ula-revenue) for affordable housing construction, subsidies for cash-strapped renters and legal assistance for tenants facing eviction. It is by far the largest single contributor to the city’s overall homelessness spending (https://homelessdashboard.lacontroller.app/).
But ULA has its critics. Not just a tax on mansions, the high rates apply to commercial, industrial and multifamily residential projects too, including land sales for new apartment developments. Apartment construction has indeed slowed to a crawl (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2025-10-01/apartment-development-pipeline-dries-up-in-spite-of-demand-for-housing) across the city in recent years and developers (https://therealdeal.com/la/2025/09/12/measure-ula-drives-developers-to-acquisitions-outside-city/?utm_campaign=sl-la-weekly&utm_source=trd-newsletter&tpcc=sl-la-weekly&utm_medium=email&utm_term=Los%20Angeles%20Weekly) and researchers have laid at least some of the blame on the city’s high transfer taxes which they argue has driven new construction down further than in surrounding cities. One report (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/7jg7m22v) by researchers at UCLA and the Rand Institute estimated that the measure has resulted in 1,910 fewer apartments per year, including 168 fewer affordable units. Another study (http://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5273034) by researchers at Harvard, UC Irvine and UC San Diego, found that property tax collections fell steeply as a result of the dramatic slow down in sales, off-setting an estimated 63% of the collected transfer tax revenue, if not significantly more.
Backers of the mansion tax have taken issue (https://www.oxy.edu/sites/default/files/Research-Flaws-Undermine-Bold-Claims-Sept-2025_4.pdf) with the UCLA study in particular. They also note that the program is currently accepting applications for its first major distribution of funds, with plans to push nearly $400 million (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2025-09-05/l-a-offers-up-387-million-for-affordable-housing-projects-its-largest-pool-ever) out the door, which could ultimately ramp up affordable housing development across the city.
But there’s growing concern, both in Los Angeles and among Democrats in Sacramento, that ULA as it currently exists has become a political vulnerability — and one that could fuel the campaign behind the statewide tax busting measure.
“Measure ULA is the tail wagging the dog,” said Mott Smith, a developer and board member of the California Infill Builders Association who co-authored another study (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/9z17p49t) that found a chilling effect on the housing market. “Anyone with assets in Los Angeles is like, ‘please where can I send my check to Howard Jarvis?’”
In the final days of the California Legislative session, Mayor Karen Bass and former Assembly Speaker Bob Hertzberg tried to hammer a grand bargain into state law. Senate Bill 423 (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb423) would have exempted certain new residential developments from the tax, offering a reprieve to many multifamily housing developers. It would have also given the city more flexibility to renegotiate affordability requirements on housing projects funded by the measure, addressing concerns by some developers and financiers that ULA cash comes with too many strings attached to be of use.
The bill would have also exempted homes destroyed in the recent wildfires.
But there was a catch: The ULA tweak would only go into effect if the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association pulls its ballot measure or it fails to qualify for the ballot.
All of that ultimately proved too complicated, contentious and of questionable legality to ram through the Legislature in the final days of the session. Long Beach Sen. Lena Gonzalez and Inglewood Assemblymember Tina McKinnor, both Democrats, vowed to pick it up again in January.

But that may be too late to neuter the anti-tax campaign. The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association is already gathering signatures and raising funds (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1059890&view=received).
“This was an attempt to cut us off early in the process, but since we’re moving forward I think the attempt to leverage this is not going to prevail,” Jon Coupal, the association’s president. “Their opportunity to ambush us is now over.”
That’s given local government groups billions of reasons to worry. Along with making it more challenging to raise revenue in the future, cities with existing high transfer taxes would see them slashed. Parcel taxes currently on the books that were approved by majorities of less than two-thirds would be similarly nixed.
Cities would lose between $2 billion and $3 billion each year if the measure becomes law, according to an analysis commissioned by the League of California Cities, a lobbying group. That includes hundreds of millions of dollars in foregone funding dedicated for new housing and homelessness services in Los Angeles and Santa Monica. But it also includes hundreds of millions more for cities that don’t use these transfer dollars for new, specific purposes and projects, but simply to top up their budgets.
The City of Berkeley, for example, stands to lose between $33 million and $63 million, according to the League’s analysis. That’s the equivalent of between 15-30% of the town’s general fund.
California’s favorite fight
Californians have been having some version of this fight for nearly half a century.
In 1978, voters passed Proposition 13, which capped property taxes and put strict limits on local and state governments’ ability to raise revenue. Defending, rolling back and revising (https://calmatters.org/politics/2020/10/prop-13-family-tree/) those limits in court battles and subsequent state ballot measure campaigns is now a storied California political tradition.
The latest chapter began in 2017 when the California Supreme Court (https://calmatters.org/economy/2017/08/california-taxes-two-step/) ruled in a case against the southern California city of Upland that citizen-initiated special tax measures only need to get more than 50% of the vote to pass. Up until that point it was presumed that the required threshold was the much more electorally formidable two-thirds.
Since then cities and counties have passed two dozen of these measures by margins of less than two-thirds. That includes taxes on parcels, sales and gross receipts that have been used to fund local schools, parks, street repairs and housing and that have been put on the ballot by homeless advocates, environmentalists and organized labor groups. It also includes Measure ULA.
And since then, business groups have been clambering to close the “Upland loophole.”
“This is now the vehicle for unions and others to be able to try and pass new taxes on targeted business sectors using a majority vote,” said Lapsely. “That only hurts job growth.”
Over that same period some cities have also turned to transfer taxes as a new source of revenue. It’s a fiscal avenue only available to a select number of cities. Under state law, most municipalities max out their transfer taxes at 55 cents for every $1,000 in sale value. But for “charter cities” — local governments with their own municipal constitution — there is no upper limit. Twenty-six have taken advantage of that fiscal opportunity.
They include Santa Monica, which passed its own version of a high-value transfer tax (Measure GS) in 2022, and Los Angeles. Voters in cities across the San Francisco Bay Area have voted to make more modest or incremental hikes over the last 10 years.
Electoral hurdles to come
The transfer tax trend has particularly irked landlords and real estate developers.
Last year, they joined forces with anti-tax advocates and other business groups to rein in both types of bothersome taxation with a ballot measure. The California Supreme Court took the unusual step of striking it (https://calmatters.org/politics/2024/06/california-taxes-supreme-court-ballot/) from the 2024 ballot, ruling that it proposed too “substantial” a change to state government to be enacted by a mere ballot measure.
This year’s version is much more carefully targeted making it less likely to hit this same constitutional snag.
But even if the signature gathering effort is successful, the Howard Jarvis campaign has its work cut out for it — even for a conservative-coded measure in reliably blue California. In late 2023, the Legislature floated its own head-spinning ballot measure (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202320240aca13) that would require future initiatives that want to hike the threshold needed to pass other measures (see: the business-backed measure) to meet that same higher threshold (in this case, two-thirds) before becoming law.
That effort to hoist the Howard Jarvis Taxpayer Association on its own petard is already slated for the November 2026 election. If it passes, it would apply to any other measures also on the ballot.

Here are the PD Editorial Board recommendations for the Nov. 3 election.
Federal
House of Representatives , District 4 — Mike Thompson
There’s a lot of pushback right now against so-called lifers in Washington, D.C. Eric Jones, who is taking on incumbent Mike Thompson is one calling out those lifers. The Press Democrat agrees with Jones and his desire to hold politicians accountable. We also recognize the need for change in Washington, but even more so we appreciate strength in stability. The Press Democrat recommends a yes vote for Mike Thompson for California’s 4th Congressional District. We think Jones has great ideas, but we recommend he gain experience at the municipal or county level first; his communities would greatly benefit. The Press Democrat endorses Mike Thompson for California’s 4th Congressional District.
To read our complete editorial, click here. (https://www.pressdemocrat.com/2026/10/06/endorsement-californias-4th-congressional-district-deserves-experience-mike-thompson-will-deliver/)
House of Representatives, 1st District — Mike McGuire
Mike McGuire is a lifelong North Coast resident and brings deep experience at every level of government, having served as a state senator, a Sonoma County supervisor, a Healdsburg city councilman and, beginning at age 19, a Healdsburg school board member. McGuire is one of California’s most effective legislators, the first rural representative to lead the upper house as president pro tem in a half-century, and after disasters in Sonoma, Mendocino and Lake counties, he is authority on wildfire prevention and recovery. He’s ready to represent the North Coast in Congress.
To read our complete editorial, click here. (https://www.pressdemocrat.com/2026/05/06/pd-editorial-mcguire-is-top-pick-for-new-house-district/)
State measures
Prop 1: Funds for housing programs — No
California needs more housing, and Prop. 1 would throw $11.25 billion at the problem without addressing the underlying causes of the state’s housing shortage and high costs. Lawmakers took the easy route. Rather than pass controversial reforms or find money in the budget, they chose to ask voters to borrow.
To read our complete editorial, click here (https://www.pressdemocrat.com/2026/10/14/endorsement-props-1-and-38-would-only-bring-more-debt-for-california/).
Prop 3 : High-income tax — Yes
This measure would make permanent higher income tax rates that voters first approved in 2012 to support education and extended in 2016. Those rates would otherwise expire in 2031. The higher rates apply only to income above $371,000 for single filers and $742,000 for joint filers. Those are 2025 thresholds and are adjusted annually for inflation. Letting them expire would amount to a huge tax cut for high earners in 2031 that would cost the state up to $15 billion annually, much of it for K-12 schools and community colleges. The Press Democrat recommends a yes vote.
To read our complete editorial, click here (https://www.pressdemocrat.com/2026/10/02/endorsement-vote-yes-on-propositions-40-and-3-so-the-wealthy-pay-a-fair-share-to-help-all-californians/).
Prop 4: Public fundraising — No
A yes vote on California Prop. 4 would allow public officers and candidates to accept public funds — taxpayer dollars — for campaign purposes. A yes vote would allow state and local governments to create programs so that public funds — again, taxpayer dollars — could be set aside for election campaigns. The Press Democrat recommends voting no on Prop. 4. Our tax dollars should not be spent on election campaigns.
To read our complete editorial, click here (https://www.pressdemocrat.com/2026/09/18/pd-endorsement-no-on-prop-4-taxpayer-dollars-should-not-support-campaigns/).
Prop. 38: Immunology Research — No
Immunology and immunotherapy hold real promise, but Prop. 38 is the wrong way to fund research into them. If California wants to fund it, the state ought to do so through the regular budget process, weighing its value against other state priorities, not with a special bond that will cost taxpayers $500 million to $600 million per year.
To read our complete editorial, click here (https://www.pressdemocrat.com/2026/10/14/endorsement-props-1-and-38-would-only-bring-more-debt-for-california/).
Prop. 39: Voter ID — No
It’s possible to view Prop. 39 and say, “What’s the big deal?” Thirty-six states require voters to present identification before voting in person. Well, the big deal is that a lot of eligible people might not be able to vote if the measure is passed. Millions of Californians wouldn’t have the ID required to satisfy this proposal. (They’d have to request a new one.) And, as the No on Prop. 39 campaign pointed out to us, when Texas implemented similar mail-ballot ID rules, rejections shot up from 1% to 12%.
To read our complete editorial, click here (https://www.pressdemocrat.com/2026/10/16/endorsement-reject-proposition-39-voter-id-fraud-ballot-measure/).
Prop 40: Billionaire tax — Yes
This measure proposes imposing a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of about 200 billionaires who lived in the state on Jan. 1, 2026. They could pay that in installments over five years. It isn’t a permanent fix to the state’s budget issues, but the cash infusion could pay for doctors, nurses, hospitals and clinics that serve people who cannot afford health care otherwise. The Press Democrat recommends a yes vote on Prop. 40.
To read our complete editorial, click here (https://www.pressdemocrat.com/2026/10/02/endorsement-vote-yes-on-propositions-40-and-3-so-the-wealthy-pay-a-fair-share-to-help-all-californians/).
Prop. 41: Tax audits — No
The measure claims to be an accountability measure that would require better auditing of new special taxes and compliance with the state’s voter-approved spending limit. California has plenty of cases of spending racing out of control without much accountability, but Prop. 41 uses that as a diversion. The Press Democrat recommends a no vote on Prop. 41.
To read our complete editorial, click here. (https://www.pressdemocrat.com/2026/10/10/endorsement-if-you-support-the-billionaire-tax-vote-no-on-props-41-and-42/)
Prop. 42: Property taxes — No
The proposed measure would ban any new state tax on personal property enacted after Jan. 1, 2026. Taxes like, say, Prop. 40’s billionaire tax. It would also prohibit taxes that apply retroactively. The more troubling part of the measure is that it would take an entire class of taxes off the table for good. The Press Democrat recommends a no vote on Prop. 42.
To read our complete editorial, click here. (https://www.pressdemocrat.com/2026/10/10/endorsement-if-you-support-the-billionaire-tax-vote-no-on-props-41-and-42/)
Prop. 43: Tax threshold — No
Proposition 43 would amend the state constitution to require two-thirds approval for special taxes proposed by residents, the requirement that special taxes proposed by local governments now face. If voters approve it, that change would apply to measures passed after Jan. 1, 2027. It aims to tackle what supporters call a “loophole” in the rules for enacting local tax measures. The system, admittedly, is strange, but it works. We recommend Californians vote no on Prop. 43.
To read our complete editorial, click here. (https://www.pressdemocrat.com/2026/10/03/endorsement-prop-43-wants-to-fix-a-system-that-isnt-broken/)
Prop. 44: Clinic funding — No
Proposition 44 would require community clinics to spend at least 90% of their revenue on patient care and the services that support it, and to report publicly how their money is spent. No more than 10% can go to executive pay, administration and overhead. But the measure would set strict spending requirements for nonprofit health clinics that could put precious revenue at risk. The Press Democrat recommends a no vote on Prop. 44.
To read our complete editorial, click here. (https://www.pressdemocrat.com/2026/09/26/endorsement-no-on-prop-44-politics-dont-belong-in-californias-community-health-clinics/)
Prop 45: CEQA Reform — No
The ballot measure seeks to streamline the current CEQA process by giving agencies 365 business days to decide on the “report card” for projects the measures define as essential, including housing, roads, water, broadband and wildfire mitigation. The measure also requires courts to resolve any cases within 270 calendar days and limit public comment to 45 days. The Press Democrat recognizes the need for reducing the state’s red tape in development, but Prop. 45 is not the way to do it.
To read our complete editorial, click here (https://www.pressdemocrat.com/2026/10/21/endorsement-no-on-prop-45-leave-states-landmark-environmental-review-law-alone/).
State candidates
Lieutenant governor — Fiona Ma
Among the two candidates left on the Nov. 3 ballot — Fiona Ma, a Democrat, and Gloria Romero, a Republican — who could lead this state’s 40 million people and oversee its $4 trillion economy? The only answer is Ma. What convinces us that Ma can actually move the needle on her agenda items is the fact that she has already been knee-deep advancing them in a senior executive capacity. The Press Democrat endorses Fiona Ma.
To read our complete editorial, click here (https://www.pressdemocrat.com/2026/09/29/endorsement-elect-fiona-ma-californias-lieutenant-governor/).
State treasurer — Eleni Kounalakis
California’s next treasurer should expect to inherit the most financially volatile environment since the Great Recession. Of the two candidates on Californians’ Nov. 3 ballots — Eleni Kounalakis, a Democrat, and Jennifer Hawks, a Republican — we support the one whose résumé instills confidence, not the one who has repeatedly declined to share her résumé. That is Kounalakis. The Press Democrat endorses Elena Kounalakis.
To read our complete editorial, click here (https://www.pressdemocrat.com/2026/10/02/endorsement-elect-eleni-kounalakis-californias-next-treasurer-2/).

Well, the big deal is that a lot of eligible people might not be able to vote if the measure is passed. Millions of Californians wouldn’t have the ID required to satisfy this proposal. (They’d have to request a new one.) And, as the No on Prop. 39 campaign pointed out to us, when Texas implemented similar mail-ballot ID rules, rejections shot up from 1% to 12%.
To read our complete editorial, click here (https://www.pressdemocrat.com/2026/10/16/endorsement-reject-proposition-39-voter-id-fraud-ballot-measure/).
Prop 40: Billionaire tax — Yes
This measure proposes imposing a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of about 200 billionaires who lived in the state on Jan. 1, 2026. They could pay that in installments over five years. It isn’t a permanent fix to the state’s budget issues, but the cash infusion could pay for doctors, nurses, hospitals and clinics that serve people who cannot afford health care otherwise. The Press Democrat recommends a yes vote on Prop. 40.
To read our complete editorial, click here (https://www.pressdemocrat.com/2026/10/02/endorsement-vote-yes-on-propositions-40-and-3-so-the-wealthy-pay-a-fair-share-to-help-all-californians/).
Prop. 41: Tax audits — No
The measure claims to be an accountability measure that would require better auditing of new special taxes and compliance with the state’s voter-approved spending limit. California has plenty of cases of spending racing out of control without much accountability, but Prop. 41 uses that as a diversion. The Press Democrat recommends a no vote on Prop. 41.
To read our complete editorial, click here. (https://www.pressdemocrat.com/2026/10/10/endorsement-if-you-support-the-billionaire-tax-vote-no-on-props-41-and-42/)
Prop. 42: Property taxes — No
The proposed measure would ban any new state tax on personal property enacted after Jan. 1, 2026. Taxes like, say, Prop. 40’s billionaire tax. It would also prohibit taxes that apply retroactively. The more troubling part of the measure is that it would take an entire class of taxes off the table for good. The Press Democrat recommends a no vote on Prop. 42.
To read our complete editorial, click here. (https://www.pressdemocrat.com/2026/10/10/endorsement-if-you-support-the-billionaire-tax-vote-no-on-props-41-and-42/)
Prop. 43: Tax threshold — No
Proposition 43 would amend the state constitution to require two-thirds approval for special taxes proposed by residents, the requirement that special taxes proposed by local governments now face. If voters approve it, that change would apply to measures passed after Jan. 1, 2027. It aims to tackle what supporters call a “loophole” in the rules for enacting local tax measures. The system, admittedly, is strange, but it works. We recommend Californians vote no on Prop. 43.
To read our complete editorial, click here. (https://www.pressdemocrat.com/2026/10/03/endorsement-prop-43-wants-to-fix-a-system-that-isnt-broken/)
Prop. 44: Clinic funding — No
Proposition 44 would require community clinics to spend at least 90% of their revenue on patient care and the services that support it, and to report publicly how their money is spent. No more than 10% can go to executive pay, administration and overhead. But the measure would set strict spending requirements for nonprofit health clinics that could put precious revenue at risk. The Press Democrat recommends a no vote on Prop. 44.
To read our complete editorial, click here. (https://www.pressdemocrat.com/2026/09/26/endorsement-no-on-prop-44-politics-dont-belong-in-californias-community-health-clinics/)

The ballot measure seeks to streamline the current CEQA process by giving agencies 365 business days to decide on the “report card” for projects the measures define as essential, including housing, roads, water, broadband and wildfire mitigation. # Revisiting the effect of supermajority requirements on fiscal outcomes
### Abstract
I use matching methods on a panel of U.S. states over the period 1960–2008 to test whether the adoption of a supermajority requirement impacts state-level expenditures and tax revenue.
While two-way fixed effects (TWFE) models show that general expenditures, welfare expenditures, and total tax revenue per capita are lower following adoption of a supermajority requirement, I also find evidence of heterogeneous treatment effects, and worse, violation of the common trends assumption.
Matching estimates fail to support the conclusions of the TWFE models, suggesting that supermajority requirements do not have a robust effect on government expenditures or tax revenue.

# Revisiting the effect of supermajority requirements on fiscal outcomes
### Abstract
I use matching methods on a panel of U.S. states over the period 1960–2008 to test whether the adoption of a supermajority requirement impacts state-level expenditures and tax revenue.
While two-way fixed effects (TWFE) models show that general expenditures, welfare expenditures, and total tax revenue per capita are lower following adoption of a supermajority requirement, I also find evidence of heterogeneous treatment effects, and worse, violation of the common trends assumption.
Matching estimates fail to support the conclusions of the TWFE models, suggesting that supermajority requirements do not have a robust effect on government expenditures or tax revenue.

Endorsement: Back Prop. 43 to restore voter-approved restrictions on local taxes
Californians have already approved these limits twice, only to have courts erode the will of the electorate

By The Mercury News/East Bay Times Editorial Boards (https://www.mercurynews.com/author/the-mercury-newseast-bay-times-editorial-boards/)
PUBLISHED: October 17, 2026 at 4:30 AM PDT | UPDATED: October 19, 2026 at 11:22 AM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
California voters have twice approved initiatives making it harder to raise local government taxes — only to have the courts erode them.
Proposition 43 would undo the latest judicial meddling by once again restoring a supermajority threshold for passage of special taxes. Voters should approve it.
There are primarily two types of local taxes:
• A general tax can be used for any legitimate government purpose and is often sought to bolster the budget of a cash-strapped agency.
• A special tax is restricted to a specific purpose such as the construction of a government building or the funding of public transit.
It’s the voting rules for the latter that are at issue with Proposition 43.
Whereas general taxes require a simple majority voter approval for passage, special taxes, under Proposition 13 in 1978 and Proposition 218 in 1996, required two-thirds — until 2017.
That’s when the state Supreme Court, in an unrelated case, distinguished between measures (https://www.mercurynews.com/2019/02/19/californias-supreme-court-has-thrown-cities-and-citizens-into-chaos-over-local-taxes/) placed on the ballot through initiative signature-gathering drives and those created by local government agencies.
Building on that court-created distinction, subsequent state appellate court rulings created a two-track system for passage of special taxes: Initiative measures require simple majority approval while those created by government agencies require two-thirds approval.

As a result, initiative special tax measures that had received more than a majority support, but less than two-thirds that had been thought necessary, have passed, including one for Alameda County (https://www.mercurynews.com/2020/03/06/borenstein-fight-over-alameda-county-sales-tax-hike-just-starting/) and one in Oakland (https://www.mercurynews.com/2019/10/17/borenstein-california-needs-clarity-on-vote-requirement-for-taxes/).
This is not what voters intended in 1978 or 1996. The route to the ballot should not determine the vote threshold for passage. Proposition 43 would overturn the court rulings and restore the two-thirds requirement for passage of special taxes.
Perverse incentives
Since 2017, we’ve seen the perverse incentives the court rulings have created. Government agencies have started turning to interest groups to qualify special taxes for the ballot.
For example, Measure RTM (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/09/endorsement-no-on-measure-rtm-transit-tax-bart-manufactured-crisis-vta-doesnt-have-one/), the regional transit sales tax measure voters are currently considering, could have been placed on the ballot by the Metropolitan Transportation Commission. But the measure would have then needed two-thirds voter approval. Instead, transit labor unions and contractors helped fund (https://thevoicesf.org/the-insiders-selling-measure-rtm/) an initiative signature drive and the subsequent campaign for the measure.
Similarly, in Oakland, the city last year put out a budget projection specifying the amount of money needed to fix a structural budget deficit and labor unions (https://netfile.com/public/COAK/campaign/filingsByMeasure/214936600-Measure%20E:%20Oakland%20Public%20Safety,%20Cleanliness%20and%20Community%20Accountability%20Act%20of%202026) then qualified a property tax measure for the June ballot (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/12/endorsement-oakland-measure-e-deceitful-tax-plan-broken-promisesn-another-deceitful-oakland-tax-plan-vote-no-on-measure-e/) for roughly that amount. (Amazingly, it failed to even muster majority support as voters recognized the long string of new taxes in recent years (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/06/05/oakland-tax-measure-e-fails/) had not been used for their promised purposes.)
In each case, the only reason backers qualified the measure through the initiative process was to bypass the two-thirds requirement — to bypass the intent of Propositions 13 and 218.
Reform needed
That said, it is past time for California voters to rethink their approach to property and other local taxes.
First, there are the backwards incentives that stemmed from court interpretations of the language Proposition 13 added to the state Constitution: “Cities, Counties and special districts, by a two-thirds vote of the qualified electors of such district, may impose special taxes on such district … .” (emphasis added)
While backers intended “special taxes” to refer to any levies beyond the Proposition 13 limit of 1% of assessed value, the Supreme Court subsequently narrowed that to mean taxes for a specific purpose. That interpretation was cemented with the passage of Proposition 218.
Consequently, we now distinguish between special taxes for specific purposes that require two-thirds approval (unless qualified through an initiative signature-gathering drive) and general taxes, which require a majority vote and can be used for any legitimate government purpose.
It’s backwards: The tax measures with the fewest restrictions are the easiest to pass. That’s why we often see local governments claiming they want money for a specific purpose but placing measures on the ballot that allow any use of the money.
A glaring example this election season is Palo Alto’s Measure J (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/14/endorsement-reject-palo-alto-nov-3-measure-j-sales-tax/), placed on the ballot by the City Council there. The measure, a proposed sales tax increase that requires majority support, is purportedly to purchase and upgrade a community center. But the tax would be permanent, and a future council could use the sales tax money for any purpose.
Property tax unfairness
Second, there’s the fundamental unfairness in Proposition 13, which not only set rules for passage of local taxes but, more significantly, governs how we tax property in California. The measure limits how much the assessed value of a property used to calculate the base tax can increase annually. But it then allows for a resetting of the assessed value when a property is sold.
The result is that people in identical houses can pay vastly different property taxes depending on when they bought their homes. It’s effectively a generational transfer of burden to newer homeowners, making the cost of housing greater for recent, including first-time, buyers.
It’s time to redistribute that burden — not to add to the total collected but to apportion it fairly in a revenue-neutral way between all property owners.
Finally, the debate over the rules for passage of local taxes and for rethinking how we tax property should be carried out in a holistic fashion, not piecemeal. And it should be decided by voters, not by the courts.
In the meantime, Proposition 43 would merely restore the intent of voters who passed the two prior measures. It merits support.

Endorsement: Yes on California Proposition 43, make it harder to raise taxes

FILE – In this June 7, 1978 file photo, Paul Gann, left, and Howard Jarvis, right, celebrate as their co-authored tax initiative Proposition 13 takes a commanding lead and ultimately won in the California primary in Los Angeles. (AP Photo/File)
By The Editorial Board (https://www.ocregister.com/author/the-editorial-board/) | opinion@scng.com (mailto:opinion@scng.com)
PUBLISHED: August 9, 2026 at 9:00 AM PDT | UPDATED: August 28, 2026 at 12:16 PM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
On the California Secretary of State’s website describing qualified statewide measures for the November ballot, voters will see a three-word reference to Proposition 43 referring to “Local taxes: limitation.” (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/qualified-ballot-measures) It’s ironic the initiative that has sparked the most backroom drama in years is depicted with such little fanfare.
Prop. 43 was placed on the ballot by a panicked California Legislature after a last- minute deal was struck with the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association to pull the association’s more sweeping Local Taxpayer Protection Act from the ballot. Despite the complicated inside-the-Capitol machinations with lobbyists and lawmakers, the resulting measure is rather simple.
If voters approve it, Prop. 43 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/aca-22.pdf) would close a court created loophole that allowed some local special taxes to evade the two-thirds vote requirement — taxes for specific items such as transit, housing, flood control and parks. Specifically, tax increases that are placed on the ballot by citizens via signature-gathering.
This change would restore the threshold to the design of 1978’s tax-limiting Proposition 13. Since then, a series of bone-headed court decisions (https://www.hjta.org/california-commentary/courts-widen-the-door-to-even-more-local-taxes-in-california/) determined that voters could approve citizen-driven special tax increases by a simple majority, while maintaining the two-thirds rule for special tax increases directly placed on the ballot by local governments. This loophole led to abuses, as unions served as the cat’s paw for local officials by gathering signatures to place tax increases on the ballot and pass them with less than a two-thirds vote.
So, the bottom line: Vote yes on Proposition 43, as it will impede local governments from getting around the two-thirds vote for special taxes to bail themselves out of endless budget debacles. As the economy has stumbled and local governments have burned through “free” COVID money from Washington, D.C., municipalities increasingly are turning to bonds and tax increases (https://caltax.org/2026/03/20/voters-to-decide-fate-of-80-local-tax-and-bond-measures-in-june/) .
Money is fungible. If voters approve “special” (https://flooddistrict.marincounty.gov/question/what-is-a-special-tax/) taxes, that leaves more money in the general fund to spend as usual. That typically means bigger paychecks and pensions for powerful public-employee unions. The two-thirds vote threshold is one of the few ways that California taxpayers can at least try to force their elected officials to live within their means.
That said, we’re disappointed that the final measure doesn’t include a ban and rollback of local transfer taxes. For instance, Los Angeles’ disastrous “mansion tax” (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2025-10-01/apartment-development-pipeline-dries-up-in-spite-of-demand-for-housing) not only imposes astronomical rates on Angelenos who sell pricey homes (currently a 4% tax on homes priced above $5.4 million and 5.5% on those priced above $10.9 million) — but applies to apartment and commercial properties. Predictably, that has quashed housing production in Los Angeles.

The original initiative by HJTA banned real estate transfer taxes above a minor documentary transfer fee. Proponents ultimately pulled that initiative from the ballot at the last minute after the Legislature passed the compromise (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/) measure that deals only with the two-thirds vote issue. The Legislature also agreed to pull a separate ballot measure designed to make it harder to pass all future tax-limitation efforts, including this one. This deal to remove the transfer-tax portion of the initiative led to a split within the business coalition that had supported it.
Complicating matters further, the key Democratic lawmakers who placed the current measure on the ballot are calling for voters to reject it. They placed it there simply as a means to derail something that they viewed as far worse (https://sdvoice.info/on-your-november-ballot-proposition-43/) because it protected taxpayers even more from the predations of government and allied special interests. But voters needn’t get caught up in the back story, however interesting as insight into Sacramento’s sausage-making process.
As it stands, the final measure is praiseworthy, as it puts the brakes on local governments’ ability to collude with special interests to more easily raise your taxes. Vote yes on Prop. 43 to make it harder to raise taxes.

California voters have twice approved initiatives making it harder to raise local government taxes — only to have the courts erode them.
Proposition 43 would undo the latest rulings by once again restoring a supermajority threshold for passage of special taxes.
Unfortunately, if approved, this would make it nearly impossible in Santa Cruz County to fund essential services and is why a majority of Editorial Board members, although divided on a recommendation, endorses a No vote on 43.
There are primarily two types of local taxes:
• A general tax can be used for any legitimate government purpose and is often sought to bolster the budget of a cash-strapped agency.
• A special tax that is restricted to a specific purpose such as the construction of a government building or the funding of public transit.
It’s the voting rules for the latter that are at issue with Proposition 43. Whereas general taxes require a simple majority voter approval for passage, special taxes, under Proposition 13 in 1978 and Proposition 218 in 1996 required two-thirds — until 2017.
That’s when the state Supreme Court, in an unrelated case, distinguished between measures placed on the ballot through initiative signature-gathering drives and those created by local government agencies.
Building on that court-created distinction, subsequent court rulings created a two-track system for passage of special taxes: Initiative measures require simple majority approval while those created by government agencies require two-thirds approval.
So since the rulings, government agencies have started turning to interest groups to qualify special taxes for the ballot.
As a result, initiative special tax measures that received more than a majority support, but less than two-thirds have passed, including the “citizen’s initiative” Measure C Workforce Housing Solutions Act tax approved by 54 percent of voters in the city of Santa Cruz in November 2025. Another majority vote is in the works for the 2028 election to help fund Santa Cruz Metro. A two-thirds requirement would probably doom this measure.
No doubt, however, a majority vote on taxes is not what voters intended in 1978 or 1996.
While many voters locally and statewide are fed up with constant initiatives to raise taxes, it’s worth noting it’s long past time for voters to rethink their approach to property and other local taxes.
First, there are the backwards incentives that stemmed from court interpretations of the language Proposition 13 added to the state Constitution: “Cities, Counties and special districts, by a two-thirds vote of the qualified electors of such district, may impose special taxes on such district … .”
While backers intended “special taxes” to refer to any levies beyond the Proposition 13 limit of 1% of assessed value, the Supreme Court subsequently narrowed that to mean taxes for a specific purpose.
Consequently, we now distinguish between special taxes for specific purposes that require two-thirds approval (unless qualified through an initiative signature-gathering drive) and general taxes, which require a majority vote and can be used for any legitimate government purpose.
But this is backwards: The tax measures with the fewest restrictions are the easiest to pass. That’s why we often see local governments claiming they want money for a specific purpose but placing measures on the ballot that allow any use of the money.
In addition, there’s the fundamental unfairness in Proposition 13, which not only set rules for passage of local taxes but governs how we tax property in California. The measure limits how much the assessed value of a property used to calculate the base tax can increase annually. But it then allows for a resetting of the assessed value when a property is sold.
The result is that people in identical houses can pay vastly different property taxes depending on when they bought their homes. It’s effectively a generational transfer of burden to newer homeowners, making the cost of housing greater for recent, including first-time, buyers.
But short of reforms, Proposition 43 at this stage would create more problems than it remedies. The debate over the rules for passage of local taxes should be carried out in a holistic fashion, not piecemeal. Vote No on Proposition 43.

Endorsement: Prop 43 is absurd, but so is California’s entire system of taxation
John Blanchard/S.F. Chronicle
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 23, 2026
Clocking in at barely over a paragraph, Proposition 43 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop43-text-proposed-laws.pdf) is the most straightforward measure on California’s November ballot.
It would mandate two-thirds voter approval (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop43-110326.pdf) — up from a simple majority — for local special taxes placed on the ballot by private citizens.
Sounds simple. But the story of how it got there involves decades-long legal battles and political bloodbaths befitting “Game of Thrones.”
Despite commanding far less attention (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/california-proposition-43-22465350.php) than Prop 40, the billionaire tax, Prop 43 is almost as controversial. At the heart of both measures is a legal, logistical and moral question reverberating throughout the nation (https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/10/18/property-taxes-housing-affordability-issue-01105514?nname=california-playbook&nid=00000150-384f-da43-aff2-bf7fd35a0000&nrid=adfb3333-039f-4cee-9cbe-7aea15435a8e): Who should pay for government services, and how should those taxes work?

While Prop 40 zeroes in on the state budget, Prop 43 focuses on how local governments raise money.
Understanding the measure requires going back to 1978, when voters approved Prop 13, the brainchild of anti-tax advocate Howard Jarvis. That measure put strict caps on property taxes — local governments’ main source of revenue.
The impact was immediate and devastating. Within the first year of Prop 13’s passage, city and county governments’ property tax revenue dropped by 60%, creating a $10 billion hole, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/publications/report/3497).
Yet Prop 13 also made it more difficult for them to raise money in other ways by requiring two-thirds voter approval for local “special” taxes, which earmark funds for specific purposes. (General taxes, which don’t specify how money must be spent, can pass with a simple majority.)
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Desperate to maintain core services such as police and fire departments — and daunted by the two-thirds threshold — local governments attempted to raise funds through assessments and property-related “fees.”
The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association fought back. In 1996, voters approved the group’s Prop 218 (https://lao.ca.gov/1996/120196_prop_218/understanding_prop218_1296.html), which made it harder for local governments to use those alternative methods.
So, to keep services running, California started picking up the tab.
Before Prop 13, local governments largely funded public education. Now, the state dedicates 40% of its budget to education. Yet with Prop 13 effectively choking off the most stable source of revenue — property taxes — California is forced to rely on income taxes from the wealthiest 1% of taxpayers, (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-taxes-proposition-3-22435509.php) which fluctuate wildly with the stock market.
With the perennial instability of state funding assistance, local governments are still struggling. Along with interest groups, they’ve repeatedly tried to punch holes in Prop 13.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
A major breakthrough occurred in 2017, when the California Supreme Court issued a ruling (https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/CA-Supreme-Court-makes-it-a-bit-easier-for-tax-12112661.php), known as the Upland decision, that found the two-thirds voter approval requirement only applies to special taxes placed on the ballot by local governments. If private citizens gather signatures for a special local tax initiative, it only needs a simple majority to pass.
Suddenly, a new revenue pathway was open.
In 2018, 61% of San Francisco voters cast ballots in favor of Prop C, which taxed large businesses to fund homeless services. That was less than two-thirds, but because private citizens — not the Board of Supervisors — placed it on the ballot, the state Supreme Court cleared the city to spend the money (https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/Calif-Supreme-Court-lets-2018-s-Prop-C-stand-15555452.php).
So, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association went to battle once again.
The group qualified a measure (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/21-0042A1%20%28Taxes%29.pdf) for the 2024 ballot that would have retroactively invalidated local special taxes that passed with less than a two-thirds vote. It would also have created additional layers of voter approvals for state and local taxes.

Article continues below this ad
When the California Supreme Court reviewed the Jarvis measure (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/jerry-brown-ballot-18643109.php) at the behest of Democratic lawmakers, however, justices found it too far-reaching and yanked it from the ballot (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/tax-ballot-measure-19520534.php).
So, Jarvis came back with a more tailored effort (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/measure-ula-howard-jarvis-ballot-mansion/) — this time backed by influential developers, businesses and real-estate groups.
It aimed to overturn the Upland ruling — and invalidate special taxes that had passed with less than a supermajority since 2017. It also proposed a strict cap on local transfer taxes — overriding those in 26 charter cities, including San Francisco and Los Angeles.
Staring at a multibillion-dollar budget crater for local governments, (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/fiscal-impact-estimate-report%2825-0006A1%29.pdf) Assembly Member Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland, introduceda bill to constrain local transfer taxes (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260ab736), although not as stringently as the initiative would have. This appeased the developers who largely funded the measure.
But Jarvis refused to withdraw it. The group’s main priority, vice president of communications Susan Shelley told us, was reversing the Upland decision.

Article continues below this ad
Ultimately, a deal was struck (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/).
Jarvis agreed to withdraw its measure — leaving transfer taxes intact — in exchange for lawmakers sending a replacement to the ballot that required all future citizen-led local special taxes to pass with a two-thirds supermajority. Lawmakers also withdrew their own ballot measure (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202320240aca13) — aimed at neutering Jarvis — that would have required any initiative mandating a two-thirds vote to itself be approved by two-thirds.
That is the head-spinning story of how we ended up with Prop 43.
So, how should voters evaluate this chimera of a measure?
On its face, it’s undemocratic to permit a minority of voters to block local special taxes supported by a majority.
At the same time, it’s hard to dispute that a lower threshold for private citizens has unleashed a wave of kooky measures with ripple effects that range from hamstringing legislators’ ability to close deficits to advancing horrible policy (see Prop I on San Francisco’s ballot (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-i-housing-san-francisco-22459341.php)).
Nor do we buy opponents’ argument that Prop 43 would be a death knell for local governments. Life existed in California before the 2017 Upland ruling. If a tax is needed and the plans are sound, voters will support it. Los Angeles County is building a multibillion-dollar transit system thanks to 2016’s Measure M, (https://www.metro.net/about/measure-m/) which passed with over 71% of the vote.
Moreover, consider the parcel tax on Oakland’s June ballot, which labor groups framed as existential for the city’s ability to fund firefighters and police officers (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/oakland-tax-measure-e-22278781.php). When voters rejected the measure, the city still balanced its budget (https://www.cbsnews.com/sanfrancisco/news/oakland-measure-e-parcel-tax/) — and avoided closing fire stations — without the money.
Yet, dissatisfied with their existing salaries and benefits, thousands of Oakland city workers, including police and fire dispatchers, recently voted to go on strike (https://www.seiu1021.org/article/votes-are-we-have-voted-overwhelmingly-strike).
A similar situation is occurring in San Francisco. Even as Mayor Daniel Lurie warns of an impending doom loop for Muni if voters don’t approve the Prop H parcel tax (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-h-muni-san-francisco-22456325.php) in November, his administration offered city workers, including Muni drivers, 12% raises over the next four years (https://www.sfchronicle.com/sf/article/sf-union-contracts-raise-city-workers-22422968.php), with a promise of no layoffs.
These examples point to an uncomfortable truth: Ballot measures are increasingly seen as cash grabs. Policymakers often feel they have no choice but to grant unsustainable salary increases and benefits — because they can pay for them with bottomless ballot campaigns.
Local governments would arguably benefit from the leverage Prop 43 would provide to keep spending in check.
Yet the measure is ultimately not a solution.
Prop 13 was intended to stymie unsustainable spending. But the budget instability it created, combined with California’s direct democracy and penchant for deceptive ballot measures (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-44-california-health-clinic-22433656.php), has created a monstrous, incoherent system of loopholes and backroom deals.
California is living in a mess of our own making. Whether or not Prop 43 passes is less significant than its mere existence.
We need comprehensive tax reform.
The states with the best outcomes — like Massachusetts — don’t have citizen tax measures. Local governments don’t need them because their states have built stable tax structures to maintain robust public services with reasonable restraints to ensure spending doesn’t get out of control.

Below, an anti-tax advocate says Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/) solidifies a constitutional amendment passed decades ago that the courts muddied. The opposing view: A city councilmember from Sonoma believes Prop. 43 enables minority rule (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-43-taxes-minority-rule/), making it harder to fund vital government functions . Guest Commentary written by Susan Shelley Susan Shelley is the vice president of communications for the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association. The November ballot measure Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/) would make it harder to raise taxes in California by restoring the two-thirds vote requirement for local special taxes. A “special tax” is one that earmarks the revenue for specific purposes. Ever since voters approved Proposition 13 in 1978 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_13,_Tax_Limitations_Initiative_(June_1978)), the California Constitution has clearly stated that cities, counties and special districts may impose special taxes “by a two-thirds vote of the qualified electors of such district.” If courts had enforced that plain language, Californians today would not be paying billions of dollars in local taxes. This includes sales tax increases such as L.A. County’s 2024 Measure A (https://homeless.lacounty.gov/measure-a/) for homelessness programs, as well as Measure ULA in the city of Los Angeles (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/), a real estate transfer tax on the value of a property worth more than $5 million, which also pays for homelessness programs and affordable housing. Neither of these received the constitutionally required 66.67% of the vote. In San Francisco, courts upheld a June 2018 special tax (http://sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/Calif-appeals-court-upholds-S-F-s-commercial-15903302.php) on commercial real estate leases to fund early education and child care, and a November 2018 special tax on the gross receipts of businesses to pay for homelessness programs. Just like Los Angeles, these measures fell short of a two-thirds vote. In 1978, the people of California added the two-thirds vote requirement for special taxes to their constitution. When did the constitution become merely advisory? READ NEXT Commentary (https://calmatters.org/category/commentary/) Minority rule in California? How Proposition 43 would tie the hands of local governments (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-43-taxes-minority-rule/) It began in 2017 with ambiguous language in a California Supreme Court decision, California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland (https://cases.justia.com/california/supreme-court/2017-s234148.pdf?ts=1503939675) . The court suggested — without really deciding — that if a tax increase was placed on the ballot by a citizens’ initiative instead of by a city council or other government body, the constitution didn’t necessarily apply, and a two-thirds vote wasn’t necessarily required. Lower courts used that language to uphold special taxes that received less than a two-thirds vote if they were placed on the ballot by voters signing initiative petitions. But who are these citizens who want to stand outside grocery stores and farmer’s markets with clipboards to raise their own taxes? They’re often the people who will get the money from the tax. The Upland decision has essentially enabled special interest groups (https://calmatters.org/economy/2019/02/local-tax-chaos-california-supreme-court/) to write their own tax increase, direct all the money to themselves, pay to collect the signatures to get it on the ballot, and then evade the two-thirds vote requirement. Some of the court rulings on these Upland taxes have even allowed local government officials to work hand-in-glove with special interests (https://www.hjta.org/california-commentary/the-fiction-of-citizens-tax-initiatives-in-california/) to get tax increases on the ballot as “citizens’ initiatives.” Now the state government is pushing the envelope even further. The governor recently signed Assembly Bill 1923 (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260ab1923), requiring the Fresno County Registrar of Voters to place a citizens’ initiative sales tax increase for transportation on the November ballot (https://fresnoland.org/2026/08/06/better-roads/). The state did this over the objections of the Fresno County Board of Supervisors after it lawfully exercised its discretion under the elections code to order a study of the measure, which would have delayed it past the 2026 ballot deadline and placed it on the 2028 ballot. This is no way to run a railroad. There is no “citizens’ initiative tax increase exception” from the two-thirds vote requirement in Prop. 13. Courts have simply made it up. Californians who are already struggling with the high cost of living have been forced to pay even higher prices because judges have made it easier to raise taxes. Prop. 43 will restore the two-thirds vote requirement for all local special taxes, including any tax increases placed on the ballot by a citizens’ initiative. It’s a constitutional amendment, overriding court precedents that say otherwise. General taxes, such as those that direct the revenue into a city or county general fund to be spent as elected officials decide, would continue to require only a simple majority vote. Some local government officials may believe voters will not approve general taxes, so they would prefer to tell voters the money from a new tax will be spent only on a specific, urgent need. Their problem isn’t the constitution, it’s trust — if voters don’t trust local elected officials to spend tax money on the most important priorities first, a majority may vote ‘no’ on any tax unless they know what it will fund and it’s guaranteed in writing. Those same officials undoubtedly benefit from having a court-created loophole to raise special taxes without the need for a two-thirds vote. The loophole has been growing with every election. Multiple “citizens’ initiative” tax increases are on the November ballot, racing to squeeze through the opening before voters can hammer boards over it. Prop. 43 gives California voters the opportunity to restore what state courts have eroded: a taxpayer protection in the state constitution that requires local special taxes to have the approval of two-thirds of voters to pass. Guest Commentary written by Sandra Lowe Sandra Lowe is a member of the Sonoma City Council and a longtime political consultant. Sometimes things that sound simple are not. Let’s take Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/). Buried in the list of ballot questions this November that could shape our tax code and California’s progress is an effort to strike a blow to the most fundamental democratic principle which guides our local governments’ decisions: majority rule. Local government is elected by majority, pass policy by majority, approve construction projects by majority and, yes, pass taxes by majority. Prop. 43 raises the threshold for local tax measures from a simple majority to two-thirds, allowing the minority to win. It must be rejected. In Sonoma County, one of the highest fire-risk areas in California, citizens passed Measure H (https://sonomacounty.gov/administrative-support-and-fiscal-services/county-executives-office/strategic-initiatives/fire-services-project/measure-h) in 2024. Measure H raises revenue through a half-cent sales tax to support emergency services. The dedicated funding ensures sustainable fire response, expanded paramedic availability and aggressive wildfire prevention. In addition to my role as a Sonoma city councilwoman, I serve on the Measure H oversight committee. Last year we were able to expand 24/7 emergency medical response teams, implement vegetation management, provide emergency response during flooding, update fire engines, provide more protective gear, install new technologies to improve firefighting capabilities and initiate community education programs. If Prop. 43 was law two years ago, none of that would have happened — even with almost 62% of the vote (https://ballotpedia.org/Sonoma_County,_California,_Measure_H,_Fire_Prevention_and_Disaster_Response_Sales_Tax_Measure_(March_2024)). Proposition 43 cleans up their mistake (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/california-constitution-proposition-43-taxes/) The largest portion of local budgets is public safety. Fire, sheriff and police services are the basics. We don’t have to look too far in our recent history to find catastrophic events which demanded the expert heroic services of our first responders. No one wants to see response times increase. No one wants to surplus an ambulance or a fire engine. Sonoma County, Altadena, Pacific Palisades — these are not rarities in a world where climate disasters are frequent. Local governments must not lose the ability to fund vital functions. The broad range of services Californians are accustomed to receiving could be slashed. Prop. 43’s unfair threshold would have doomed measures such as Alameda County’s 2025 measure for healthcare funding (https://health.alamedacountyca.gov/program/measures-a-c-and-w/) and Santa Clara’s June measure for open space preservation (https://www.openspaceauthority.org/whats-new/press-release-measure-d). Citizens have high expectations for local government. They expect us to deliver a wide range of services. Prop. 43 would tie the hands of local governments statewide, allowing a slim minority to determine the outcomes of ballot issues and disenfranchise voters. Prop. 43 would take us backward and begin round after round of service cuts, potentially making California less protected from disasters and more vulnerable to crime. Minority rule in California? How Proposition 43 would tie the hands of local governments

By Sandra Lowe, Special for CalMatters

This commentary was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

California voters will get to decide in November if it should be harder to pass tax measures at the local level. Below, a city councilmember from Sonoma believes Proposition 43 enables minority rule, making it harder to fund vital government functions. The opposing view: An anti-tax advocate says Prop. 43 solidifies a constitutional amendment passed decades ago that the courts muddied.

Guest Commentary written by

Sometimes things that sound simple are not. 

Let’s take Proposition 43. Buried in the list of ballot questions this November that could shape our tax code and California’s progress is an effort to strike a blow to the most fundamental democratic principle which guides our local governments' decisions: majority rule.  

Local government is elected by majority, pass policy by majority, approve construction projects by majority and, yes, pass taxes by majority.

Prop. 43 raises the threshold for local tax measures from a simple majority to two-thirds, allowing the minority to win. It must be rejected.

In Sonoma County, one of the highest fire-risk areas in California, citizens passed Measure H in 2024. Measure H raises revenue through a half-cent sales tax to support emergency services. The dedicated funding ensures sustainable fire response, expanded paramedic availability and aggressive wildfire prevention. In addition to my role as a Sonoma city councilwoman, I serve on the Measure H oversight committee.

Last year we were able to expand 24/7 emergency medical response teams, implement vegetation management, provide emergency response during flooding, update fire engines, provide more protective gear, install new technologies to improve firefighting capabilities and initiate community education programs. 

If Prop. 43 was law two years ago, none of that would have happened — even with almost 62% of the vote.

The largest portion of local budgets is public safety. Fire, sheriff and police services are the basics. We don’t have to look too far in our recent history to find catastrophic events which demanded the expert heroic services of our first responders.

No one wants to see response times increase. No one wants to surplus an ambulance or a fire engine. Sonoma County, Altadena, Pacific Palisades — these are not rarities in a world where climate disasters are frequent.

Local governments must not lose the ability to fund vital functions.

The broad range of services Californians are accustomed to receiving could be slashed. Prop. 43’s unfair threshold would have doomed measures such as Alameda County’s 2025 measure for healthcare funding and Santa Clara’s June measure for open space preservation.  

Citizens have high expectations for local government. They expect us to deliver a wide range of services. Prop. 43 would tie the hands of local governments statewide, allowing a slim minority to determine the outcomes of ballot issues and disenfranchise voters. Prop. 43 would take us backward and begin round after round of service cuts, potentially making California less protected from disasters and more vulnerable to crime.

Majority rule is the basis of our democracy and a hallmark of a free society. Let's not go backward.

California is about to have a massive fight over taxes. Here’s why Los Angeles is the frontline

In summary
A low-tax advocacy group seems intent on making the Los Angeles “mansion tax” the face of their statewide tax-capping ballot measure campaign.
Welcome to CalMatters, the only nonprofit newsroom devoted solely to covering issues that affect all Californians. Sign up for WhatMatters (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/whatmatters) to receive the latest news and commentary on the most important issues in the Golden State.
In 2022, the Los Angeles electorate voted to slap the sale of mansions and other high-value real estate deals across the city with a hefty tax.
Locals have been debating Measure ULA ever since. Supporters call it a vital lifeline for the city’s unhoused and housing insecure who stand to benefit from the hundreds of millions of dollars the initiative has already raked in. Critics call it an economic own-goal that has choked off new apartment construction in a city where new housing is in excruciatingly short supply.
That debate is about to go statewide.
The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, a low tax advocacy group, is currently gathering signatures to put a measure on California’s November 2026 ballot. A central part of their pitch: No more Measure ULAs.
The proposed constitutional amendment takes aim at two types of taxation common across California:
Transfer taxes on the sale of real estate. The measure would cap rates at a little more than one-twentieth of one percent of the value of the property. Los Angeles’ highest rate is one hundred-times higher.
Local tax measures put on the ballot by voter-backed campaigns (as opposed to those put there by city councils) that are earmarked for a particular purpose. The tax-capping proposal would raise the electoral support needed to pass these types of “special” tax measures to two-thirds, up from a simple majority of more than 50%.
Municipal governments across the state stand to lose billions of dollars (with taxpayers standing to save just as much) if the measure ultimately succeeds. Voter-proposed tax hikes have been approved by simple majorities in cities and counties across California. Transfer tax hikes have also been a popular funding source for certain local governments.
Measure ULA, which 58% of Los Angeles voters backed in 2022, happens to be both. The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association and its political allies appear happy to make it the face of the statewide campaign.
Putting a lid on both citizen-initiated tax measures and high transfer taxes “is something that we have always had as a priority,” said Rob Lapsely, president of the California Business Roundtable, a coalition that has yet to take a formal position on the measure but which backed an earlier version. “The question was, ‘can we actually find the right opportunity?’”
“And then suddenly, along came Measure ULA.”
The fight over the “mansion tax”
The City of Los Angeles’ measure was sold to voters as a “mansion tax,” because it sticks new, elevated transfer fee rates on only the highest value sales: 4% on properties between $5 million and $10 million and 5.5% for those above that. Those numbers have inched up with inflation. All sales below those thresholds are taxed at roughly half of one percent.
